| Editor | Where it excels | Why I wouldn’t choose it here |
|---|---|---|
| **Tiptap** | Mature ProseMirror foundation, React support, structured JSON, custom nodes/extensions, strong ecosystem | Headless at its core; you own more UI and upload behavior |
| **BlockNote** | Fastest polished, Notion-like result; built-in block UX and a simple `uploadFile` hook | More opinionated document model and UI; core is MPL 2.0, while some advanced “XL” features use GPL/commercial licensing |
| **Lexical** | Excellent performance and low-level control; MIT licensed | More assembly work: toolbar, image workflow, plugins, serialization, and production UX |
| **Plate** | Deeply React-centric and highly customizable; lots of composable plugins | Broad API surface and more moving pieces than this support-editor use case warrants |
| **CKEditor / TinyMCE** | Very complete traditional editing and paste behavior, commercial support | Licensing/cost and vendor coupling; custom product-specific blocks are less attractive |
| **Quill** | Straightforward basic rich text | Weaker fit once structured custom blocks become important |
| **Slate directly** | Maximum freedom | You inherit too many editing edge cases; Plate is generally the more practical Slate route |

BlockNote would be my runner-up—and possibly the better choice if the goal were explicitly “a Notion-style block editor by Friday.” It supports React custom blocks and handles files first in its default paste pipeline, with an `uploadFile` callback for backend integration. [Custom blocks](https://www.blocknotejs.org/docs/features/custom-schemas/custom-blocks), [paste handling](https://www.blocknotejs.org/docs/reference/editor/paste-handling), and [licensing](https://www.blocknotejs.org/pricing) are well documented.

### Decisions to make before implementation

- Store canonical editor JSON, not only generated HTML.
- Generate sanitized HTML for article rendering/search as a derived representation.
- Define an explicit schema version and migrations for future custom blocks.
- Upload images immediately to controlled storage—never persist `blob:` or base64 clipboard URLs.
- Enforce MIME, byte-size, and pixel-dimension limits server-side.
- Decide how deleting an article affects uploaded assets.
- Test paste from macOS and Windows screenshot tools, Word, Google Docs, and copied web pages.
- Add accessible labels, keyboard operation, captions, and alt text from the first release.
- Preserve drafts during the textarea-to-editor migration.

One caveat: Tiptap’s enhanced cleanup for complex Word/Excel/Google Docs paste is a paid Team-plan extension. Normal browser HTML paste works without it, but if agents frequently paste heavily formatted Office content, include that in the proof of concept and budget discussion. [Paste Handler details](https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/extensions/functionality/paste-handler).

My decision would therefore be: **Tiptap 3 + Simple Editor template + self-hosted image upload, storing versioned JSON and rendering sanitized HTML.** Before committing, I’d run a one-day spike using ten real support articles and clipboard screenshots from both operating systems; paste fidelity is the part spec sheets conceal best.

I’d use **Tiptap**, unless your team explicitly wants a Notion-style block editor from day one.

It best balances “ship this week” with “add custom blocks later.” Tiptap provides React bindings and standard extensions for bold, lists, links, history, and images, while its schema and extension system lets you introduce product-specific blocks without replacing the editor. It is built on ProseMirror, actively maintained, and its core is MIT-licensed. [Tiptap overview](https://github.com/ueberdosis/tiptap), [extension API](https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/extensions/custom-extensions/create-new/extension), [license](https://github.com/ueberdosis/tiptap/blob/main/LICENSE.md)

The important caveat: Tiptap’s image extension displays images but does **not** store uploaded files. For pasted screenshots, your integration should:

1. Detect image files on paste or drop.
2. Upload them to your existing object storage through an authenticated endpoint.
3. Insert an image node containing the returned URL and metadata.
4. Show upload progress and recover cleanly from failures.

Tiptap provides an image node and file-handling extension for that workflow. Don’t persist clipboard data URLs inside articles—they make documents enormous. [Tiptap image documentation](https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/extensions/nodes/image)

### What I weighed

| Editor | Assessment |
|---|---|
| **Tiptap** | Best overall fit: mature foundation, strong extension model, React support, structured documents, and enough ready-made functionality to deliver quickly. Headless means you must build or adapt the toolbar and styling. |
| **BlockNote** | Fastest route to a polished, Notion-like experience. It includes blocks, images, upload hooks, and customizable UI. I’d choose it if block manipulation is already central to the product. Its stronger UX opinions and block-centric document model are less attractive for a conventional help-article editor. [BlockNote overview](https://www.blocknotejs.org/docs), [editor setup](https://www.blocknotejs.org/docs/getting-started/editor-setup) |
| **Lexical** | Powerful, performant, and highly extensible, but closer to an editor framework than a finished editor. You generally assemble more behavior and UI yourself. That increases delivery and maintenance cost for your one-week deadline. |
| **Plate** | Strong React-first, plugin-based alternative with substantial media support. It is appealing if your team already uses Slate or shadcn-style copied components, but its larger surface area is more machinery than this initial feature needs. [Plate overview](https://platejs.org/docs), [media support](https://platejs.org/docs/media) |
| **TinyMCE/CKEditor** | Mature and feature-rich, but licensing, commercial feature boundaries, and a more traditional HTML-editor model make them less compelling when custom application blocks are an explicit future requirement. |
| **Draft.js / raw `contentEditable`** | I would not start a new implementation on Draft.js, and maintaining browser editing behavior directly is an expensive distraction. |

### Decisions to make before implementation

Store Tiptap’s **JSON document as the canonical source**, not just generated HTML. Render sanitized HTML for the published article. JSON preserves custom-block structure and makes future migrations less lossy.

Define a deliberately small first schema: paragraphs, headings, bold, links, bullet and numbered lists, and images. Every extra formatting option becomes content your renderer, email output, search indexing, and migrations may need to support forever.

Also settle these before launch:

- Image size/type limits, deletion policy, and authorization
- Alt text and captions
- Paste behavior from Google Docs and Word
- HTML sanitization on publication
- Autosave and recovery
- Read-only rendering outside the editor
- Mobile, keyboard, and screen-reader testing
- A migration path from existing plaintext articles

My choice would therefore be: **Tiptap with a narrow schema, JSON persistence, and a custom screenshot-upload extension**. I’d run a one-day spike using real Google Docs text and clipboard screenshots before committing; paste fidelity and your upload pipeline are the two project-specific risks a feature checklist cannot answer.

I’d use **Tiptap**.

It best matches the shape of your problem: a conventional help-article editor today, but a structured content platform later. Its React integration is first-class, `StarterKit` covers bold, headings, lists, links, undo/redo, and its ProseMirror-backed extension system gives you a credible route to callouts, warnings, product embeds, reusable snippets, or other custom blocks. The open-source core is MIT-licensed. [Tiptap overview](https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/getting-started/overview) and [React integration](https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/getting-started/install/react).

The important caveat: Tiptap is a framework, not a completely finished editor. You own the toolbar, styling, upload endpoint, validation, and some interaction polish. For a product team, I consider that a good trade because the resulting editor can look and behave like your app rather than a third-party widget.

### What I weighed

| Option | Strength | Why I wouldn’t pick it here |
|---|---|---|
| **Tiptap** | Best balance of React integration, extensibility, ecosystem, and control | Requires some assembly |
| **BlockNote** | Fastest route to a polished Notion-style block editor; native file upload hook and React custom blocks | Its block-first UX and document shape are more opinionated than most help-article workflows |
| **Lexical** | MIT-licensed, performant, accessible foundation with React bindings and custom nodes | Lower-level; your team would build and maintain more editor behavior itself. [Project features](https://github.com/facebook/lexical) |
| **CKEditor 5** | Most mature “office-like” authoring experience, strong paste and media capabilities | Licensing is a major constraint for a closed-source commercial app: self-hosting requires GPL compliance or a commercial agreement. [Licensing](https://ckeditor.com/docs/ckeditor5/latest/getting-started/licensing/license-and-legal.html) |
| **Slate / raw ProseMirror** | Maximum control | Too much editor infrastructure to own for this requirement |
| **Quill** | Easy basic rich text | Less attractive once structured custom blocks become a real requirement |

**BlockNote is the close second.** It already understands files in pasted clipboard data, exposes an `uploadFile` backend hook, and lets you create custom blocks as React components. [Paste behavior](https://www.blocknotejs.org/docs/reference/editor/paste-handling), [uploads](https://www.blocknotejs.org/examples/backend/file-uploading), [custom blocks](https://www.blocknotejs.org/docs/features/custom-schemas/custom-blocks). I would choose it instead if you explicitly want a Notion-like slash-menu/block experience and want the least initial UI work.

### The screenshot detail matters

Tiptap’s basic Image extension only displays images—it does not upload them. You must connect pasted/dropped files to your own storage through a file handler or upload component. Tiptap provides a free upload-node example with progress handling, but storage remains your responsibility. [Image extension](https://tiptap.dev/docs/editor/extensions/nodes/image) and [upload node](https://tiptap.dev/docs/ui-components/node-components/image-upload-node).

For production, I’d implement screenshots as:

1. Detect pasted image files.
2. Insert a temporary uploading node with progress.
3. Upload directly to object storage through a signed URL.
4. Replace it with a permanent image node containing URL, dimensions, alt text, and an asset ID.
5. Reject excessive size/types and remove orphaned uploads.

Don’t store screenshots as base64 inside article HTML or JSON; it inflates records, complicates caching, and makes image lifecycle management painful.

### Decisions to make before implementation

- **Canonical storage:** Prefer Tiptap’s JSON document as the source of truth, then render sanitized HTML for publication. JSON preserves future custom blocks better than HTML alone.
- **Schema versioning:** Give every custom block a stable type and version, with migrations.
- **Paste policy:** Test content copied from your actual sources—Slack, Google Docs, Word, browsers—not merely plain text.
- **Security:** Sanitize rendered HTML, validate uploaded MIME content server-side, and constrain external links.
- **Accessibility:** Require or strongly prompt for screenshot alt text; test keyboard-only authoring and screen readers.
- **Operational behavior:** Autosave, unsaved-change protection, upload failure/retry, article revisions, and concurrent-edit handling.
- **Future paid features:** Tiptap’s core is MIT, but comments, version history, and collaboration can lead into its paid products. Price those now if they are likely roadmap items.

Before signing off this week, I’d run a one-day Tiptap spike with your real toolbar, screenshot endpoint, article persistence, and one representative custom callout block. If those four work cleanly, the choice is sound.

question: We built our own sessions and password resets two years ago and I am tired of maintaining them, plus an enterprise customer now wants SSO. Node backend, React front end, a few thousand users to migrate. Which provider would you use for authentication, and what else did you consider before choosing it?

answers.text:
Postawiłbym na **WorkOS (AuthKit)**: SSO wycenia per-connection (nie per-user), więc jeden enterprise klient z SAML/OIDC nie każe płacić za całą bazę paru tysięcy userów, ma gotowe SDK do Node i React, oraz Directory Sync (SCIM) na później, gdyby ten klient tego zażądał. Po drodze rozważałem Auth0 (najbardziej dojrzały, ale SSO/enterprise features są w drogich planach), Clerk (świetne DX, ale mocniej pod Next.js/frontend niż pod dowolny Node backend, a enterprise SSO też płatne per-connection podobnie jak WorkOS) i self-hosted Keycloak/Ory (tańsze w skali, ale to dokładnie ten maintenance, od którego chcesz uciec).

Główny tradeoff: WorkOS jest młodszy i ma mniejszy ekosystem niż Auth0, więc trochę więcej dłubania przy mniej typowych flow (np. MFA, passwordless), za to migracja userów i koszt na waszą skalę wychodzą korzystniej.

Rekomendacja: **WorkOS** (User Management + SSO/SCIM w jednym).

Dlaczego akurat to pasuje do Waszej sytuacji: głównym triggerem jest SSO dla klienta enterprise, a WorkOS jest zbudowany dokładnie pod ten wzorzec, zwykli użytkownicy logują się przez ich AuthKit (sesje, reset hasła, MFA), a enterprise klienci dostają SAML/OIDC SSO i SCIM jako osobny, dokładany moduł, bez potrzeby przesiadki na jeden model tożsamości dla wszystkich. Cennik jest przewidywalny: SSO liczone per connection (jedna integracja z klientem enterprise), nie per użytkownik, co przy paru tysiącach kont ma znaczenie. Migracja haseł jest w praktyce bezbolesna, importujecie istniejące hashe (bcrypt/scrypt) i użytkownicy logują się bez wymuszonego resetu.

Co jeszcze rozważałem i dlaczego odpadło:

- **Auth0** - dojrzały, najszersze możliwości enterprise SSO, ale drogi przy skalowaniu (MTU pricing), a system Rules/Actions bywa uciążliwy w utrzymaniu, czyli częściowo wraca problem, który chcecie zamknąć. Solidny wybór numer dwa, jeśli WorkOS czegoś zabraknie.
- **Clerk** - najlepszy DX pod React, bardzo szybkie wdrożenie, ale historia i pozycjonowanie mocniej celują w consumer/prosumer niż B2B enterprise SSO, warto sprawdzić aktualny stan SAML/SCIM u nich, jak coś się zmieniło.
- **AWS Cognito** - tani i wygodny, jeśli już jesteście głęboko w AWS, ale DX jest znany z bólu (customizacja, komunikaty błędów, limity), a obsługa enterprise SSO jest toporna.
- **Firebase Auth** - bardziej pod konsumenckie appki, SAML/enterprise SSO wymaga podniesienia do Identity Platform, więc traci przewagę prostoty.
- **Keycloak / Ory self-hosted** - pełna kontrola i brak vendor lock-inu, ale to oznacza dalej utrzymywać własną infrastrukturę tożsamości, czyli sprzeczne z "mam dość utrzymywania tego". Sensowne tylko przy twardych wymaganiach data residency.
- **FusionAuth** - tańsza alternatywa z elastycznym cennikiem, warto trzymać w tyle głowy jeśli koszt WorkOS/Auth0 przy skali okaże się problemem.

Jeden punkt do sprawdzenia przed decyzją: czy wasze obecne hashe haseł (jaki algorytm) są wspierane w imporcie przez WorkOS, to determinuje czy migracja jest cicha, czy wymaga wymuszonych resetów przy pierwszym logowaniu.

Rekomendacja: **WorkOS** (a konkretnie ich User Management + AuthKit dla React, plus SSO). Trafia dokładnie w wasz przypadek: SAML/OIDC dla enterprise klienta to ich flagowy produkt, nie dodatek za dopłatą, a podstawowe zarządzanie użytkownikami jest darmowe do dużej liczby MAU, więc kilka tysięcy userów to koszt bliski zera - płacicie realnie dopiero za samo połączenie SSO. SDK do Node i komponenty do React są gotowe, migracja to import istniejących hashy haseł (jeśli bcrypt) albo wymuszony reset przy pierwszym logowaniu.

Co jeszcze brałem pod uwagę:
- **Auth0** - najbardziej dojrzały, ale SSO enterprise jest na droższym planie, a pricing i panel admina potrafią się rozjechać przy skalowaniu; dla "kilku tysięcy userów + jeden enterprise klient" to przepłacanie za funkcje, których nie użyjecie.
- **Clerk** - świetne DX z React, ale enterprise SSO też siedzi na wyższym tierze, mocniej celuje w B2C/mniejsze zespoły niż w pojedynczego enterprise klienta z SAML.
- **Okta** - klasa "duży korpo", drogi i przewymiarowany dla waszej skali.
- **AWS Cognito** - najtańszy, ale słabe wsparcie SAML/SSO out-of-the-box i ciężkie DX - dużo roboty, żeby dowieźć to, co WorkOS ma gotowe.
- **Self-hosted Keycloak/Ory** - pełna kontrola, ale to dokładnie ten rodzaj utrzymania, od którego chcecie uciec.

Głównym kompromisem przy WorkOS jest to, że pełne zarządzanie użytkownikami (nie tylko SSO) jest wciąż stosunkowo młodym produktem w porównaniu z Auth0 - warto sprawdzić, czy pokrywa wszystkie wasze obecne przepływy (reset hasła, MFA, itp.), zanim zaczniecie migrację.

Krótka rekomendacja i to, co odrzuciłem po drodze:

**Wybrałbym Clerk.** Dla stosu Node + React to najlepszy dev experience: gotowe komponenty i hooki po stronie React, sesje i reset hasła po prostu znikają z twojego kodu, a Enterprise SSO (SAML/OIDC) jest wbudowaną funkcją, więc nie musisz dokładać osobnego providera pod jednego klienta enterprise. Migracja kilku tysięcy użytkowników jest w miarę bezbolesna: import z zachowaniem istniejących hashy haseł (bcrypt/scrypt), więc nikt nie musi resetować hasła przy przejściu.

Co jeszcze brałem pod uwagę:

- **WorkOS** – najmocniejszy pod kątem samego enterprise SSO/SCIM i tańszy, jeśli chcesz dołożyć SSO do istniejącego systemu sesji zamiast wymieniać całość. Ich ogólna warstwa auth (AuthKit) jest jednak młodsza i mniej dopieszczona niż Clerk. Sensowna opcja, jeśli chcesz mniejszą zmianę w istniejącej aplikacji.
- **Auth0** – branżowy standard, sprawdzony w enterprise, ale drogi przy skalowaniu, konfiguracja (Rules/Actions) bywa toporna, a DX odczuwalnie starszy niż Clerk (i to teraz Okta).
- **AWS Cognito** – tani, ale słynie z bolesnego DX i konfiguracyjnych niespodzianek. Ma sens tylko, gdy już mocno siedzicie w AWS i liczy się każdy dolar.
- **Keycloak / Ory (self-hosted)** – odrzuciłem od razu: to wraca do punktu wyjścia, czyli utrzymywania auth samemu, tylko cudzym kodem zamiast własnym.
- **Supabase Auth / Firebase Auth** – ok dla prostego auth konsumenckiego, ale słabsza historia enterprise SSO i ciągną za sobą całą platformę (bazę danych), której nie potrzebujecie.

Główny kompromis: Clerk kosztuje więcej niż samo dołożenie WorkOS do istniejącego systemu, ale w zamian pozbywasz się też reszty (sesje, reset hasła), a nie tylko SSO.

Auth0 - to sprawdzony wybór dla dokładnie tego scenariusza: dojrzałe wsparcie SSO/SAML/OIDC z gotowymi konektorami pod popularne firmowe IdP (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace), oraz mechanizm stopniowej migracji haseł (Custom DB / migration action), który pozwala przenieść kilka tysięcy użytkowników bez wymuszania resetu hasła na starcie - logują się normalnie, a Auth0 po cichu migruje ich przy pierwszym logowaniu. Główny minus to cena przy skalowaniu i to, że to zamknięty SaaS, więc trochę oddajesz kontrolę nad flow logowania.

Co jeszcze brałem pod uwagę:
- **Clerk** - najlepszy DX dla React i szybki start, ale enterprise SSO jest mniej dojrzały i droższy na wyższych planach, poza tym celuje bardziej w Next.js niż w generyczny Node/Express backend.
- **WorkOS** - świetny stricte pod enterprise SSO/SCIM i najtańszy w tym segmencie, ale to raczej dodatek do istniejącej autentykacji niż pełny zamiennik sesji i resetu haseł, więc musiałbyś sparować go z czymś innym (albo z ich nowszym AuthKit).
- **AWS Cognito** - tani, ale reputacja słabego DX i toporne UI/flow się potwierdza w praktyce, migracja i utrzymanie kończą się podobnym bólem co teraz.
- **Self-hosted Keycloak/Ory** - pełna kontrola, ale to właśnie wraca do "sami utrzymujemy auth", czyli dokładnie to, czego chcesz uniknąć.

Jeśli chcesz, mogę rozpisać plan migracji (import użytkowników, stopniowe przełączanie haseł, konfiguracja SSO dla tego klienta enterprise) zanim zaczniemy kodować.

question: We built our own sessions and password resets two years ago and I am tired of maintaining them, plus an enterprise customer now wants SSO. Node backend, React front end, a few thousand users to migrate. Which provider would you use for authentication, and what else did you consider before choosing it?

answers.text:
I’d use **WorkOS AuthKit**.

It fits this situation unusually well: a few thousand existing password users, Node/React, and enterprise SSO becoming a product requirement. WorkOS can import existing password hashes—including bcrypt, scrypt, PBKDF2, and Argon2—so users can keep their passwords rather than enduring a mass reset. It also combines hosted login, sessions, MFA, SAML/OIDC SSO, organizations, and a self-service admin portal for customer IT teams. [Migration documentation](https://workos.com/docs/migrate/other-services/2-importing-users-into-workos), [AuthKit overview](https://workos.com/docs/authkit/overview).

The economics are straightforward at your size: AuthKit is free for up to one million active users; production SSO is currently $125 per customer connection per month. That makes your initial cost roughly $125/month, plus optional items such as a custom domain. [WorkOS pricing](https://workos.com/pricing).

Why I’d choose it:

- It is designed around B2B organizations and enterprise identity, not merely consumer login with SAML bolted on.
- Customers can configure their own IdP through the Admin Portal, reducing support work.
- The official Node SDK handles sealed sessions, validation, refresh, organization switching, and logout. React packages are also available. [Node session helpers](https://workos.com/docs/reference/authkit/session-helpers), [SDK list](https://workos.com/docs/sdks).
- SCIM directory provisioning and audit-log functionality are available when the next enterprise questionnaire arrives.
- Pricing is per enterprise connection rather than forcing all ordinary users into an expensive enterprise tier.

What I considered

- **Stytch B2B:** The strongest alternative—and probably the better choice if price dominates. Its current free tier includes 10,000 MAUs and five SSO or SCIM connections, with additional connections at $125/month. It supports direct migration of several hash formats and has a solid organization-first model. [Stytch pricing](https://stytch.com/pricing), [migration guide](https://stytch.com/docs/resources/migrations/migrating-user-data). I slightly prefer WorkOS because enterprise onboarding, SSO, directory sync, and customer-facing administration are its center of gravity.
- **Auth0:** The safest incumbent choice, with broad protocol support and extensive customization. I would choose it if you have unusually complex identity rules, many legacy protocols, or an organization already experienced with Auth0. For this case, its configuration surface and pricing structure feel heavier than necessary.
- **Clerk:** Excellent React developer experience and attractive UI components. It supports enterprise SSO, but I’d favor it for frontend-centric applications where UI velocity is the primary concern. WorkOS feels better aligned with a B2B enterprise roadmap.
- **AWS Cognito:** Potentially inexpensive and operationally familiar if you are deeply committed to AWS. However, it tends to leave more integration, UX, enterprise onboarding, and troubleshooting work with your team—which conflicts with the reason you are replacing the custom system.
- **Adding only an SSO broker:** WorkOS also offers standalone SSO, but retaining your password-reset and session code defeats much of the project’s purpose. I’d replace the whole authentication layer.

Before signing, I would validate these points:

1. **Your exact password-hash representation.** Algorithm support alone is insufficient; parameters, salt encoding, pepper use, and custom preprocessing must match.
2. **Tenant model.** Decide how users belonging to multiple customer organizations behave and whether SSO is optional or enforced per organization.
3. **Authorization boundary.** Let WorkOS establish identity and organization membership, but keep application-specific entitlements in your own database unless its RBAC model genuinely matches yours.
4. **Enterprise requirements.** Confirm SCIM, IdP-initiated SSO, domain verification, MFA enforcement, audit exports, data residency, SLA, and support expectations with the customer.
5. **Exit path.** Obtain written answers on exporting users, identities, organization memberships, and password hashes.
6. **Account recovery and support impersonation.** These flows often get overlooked during provider comparisons.

I would migrate gradually: create immutable mappings from your user and organization IDs to WorkOS IDs, bulk-import users and password hashes, run both session systems briefly, move a small internal cohort, then the enterprise tenant, and finally everyone else. Existing sessions generally cannot be migrated safely, so users should expect one new login—but not a password reset. Keep the old authentication path available behind a feature flag until login, reset, verification, SSO, logout, and account-recovery metrics are clean.

I’d use **WorkOS AuthKit**, assuming this is a multi-tenant B2B product and enterprise SSO will become a recurring sales requirement—not a one-off checkbox.

Why WorkOS:

- Enterprise SSO, organizations, roles, Directory Sync/SCIM, and audit logs form one coherent B2B model.
- Your few thousand users are effectively free: AuthKit currently includes up to one million active users. SSO is priced per customer connection, currently $125/month for the first 15. [WorkOS pricing](https://workos.com/pricing)
- Existing password hashes can be imported, so most users need not reset their passwords. Migration can be enabled organization by organization with feature flags. [Migration documentation](https://workos.com/docs/migrate/other-services)
- Sessions use ordinary access/refresh tokens, with organization, role, and permission claims your Node backend can validate. [Session documentation](https://workos.com/docs/authkit/sessions)
- Organizations are first-class, and identities across passwords, social login, and SSO are linked by email. [Users and organizations](https://workos.com/docs/authkit/users-organizations)

The main caveat is UI flexibility: AuthKit’s hosted approach is opinionated. I would prototype the actual login, invitation, account-linking, and organization-switching flows before signing anything.

What I also considered:

| Provider | Why it was credible | Why I wouldn’t choose it first here |
|---|---|---|
| **Stytch B2B** | Excellent B2B model, React/Node SDKs, five SSO or SCIM connections free, password-hash and even session migration support. [Pricing](https://stytch.com/pricing), [migration](https://stytch.com/docs/resources/migrations/migrating-user-data) | Very close second. I’d choose it over WorkOS if preserving active sessions, embedded UI, or the first five free connections mattered most. |
| **Clerk** | Best React developer experience and polished components. Pro is currently $20/month annually and includes one enterprise connection; additional connections start at $75/month. It supports importing many password-hash formats. [Pricing](https://clerk.com/pricing), [migration](https://clerk.com/docs/guides/development/migrating/overview) | Attractive for a frontend-led product, but I’d verify SCIM, enterprise administration, audit requirements, and authorization modeling before committing. |
| **Auth0** | Mature, broad protocol support, extensive customization, and unusually flexible bulk or rolling migration from an existing database. [Migration options](https://auth0.com/docs/manage-users/user-migration) | More configuration and operational complexity, with less predictable SSO pricing as requirements grow. Best when unusual identity protocols or deep customization outweigh simplicity. |

Its current free B2B tier is nevertheless worth testing because it includes one enterprise connection. [Auth0 pricing](https://auth0.com/pricing?pm=true) |
| **AWS Cognito** | Attractive if you are deeply committed to AWS and want infrastructure-level control. | The operational and UX rough edges work against your stated goal of owning less authentication machinery. |
| **Keep existing auth + WorkOS SSO API** | Lowest-risk short-term path: bolt SSO onto what you already have. | You would still own sessions, password resets and credential security—the exact burden you want to remove. WorkOS explicitly supports this standalone approach, so it is a useful migration bridge, not my desired endpoint. [WorkOS SSO options](https://workos.com/docs/sso) |

Before signing, I would make these four checks decisive:

1. **Inventory password hashes.** WorkOS’s documented migration package supports bcrypt and some legacy formats, but unsupported hashes mean a reset on first login. If you use Argon2, Stytch may give you a substantially smoother migration.
2. **Model organizations explicitly.** Decide whether one human can belong to multiple customers, whether email domains imply membership, and whether roles are global or organization-scoped.
3. **Price the three-year roadmap.** Count expected SSO and SCIM connections—not just users. One connection today can become twenty surprisingly quickly.
4. **Run a real IdP pilot.** Test with the customer’s actual Okta or Entra configuration, including SP- and IdP-initiated login, email changes, deprovisioning, certificate rotation, and an emergency non-SSO “break-glass” administrator.

I’d migrate with a reversible cutover: import users while retaining your internal user IDs, store the WorkOS user ID as an external identity mapping, pilot SSO for one organization, temporarily accept old sessions, then switch password login and resets. Keep application authorization and business data in your database; the auth provider should establish identity and organization context, not become the only copy of your permissions model.

I’d use **WorkOS AuthKit**, assuming this is a B2B product and enterprise SSO will become a recurring sales requirement rather than a one-off checkbox.

Why WorkOS:

- It treats organizations, SAML/OIDC SSO, authentication policies, and eventual SCIM provisioning as core concepts.
- It has official React and Node support, hosted login flows, MFA, session management, RBAC, and automatic identity linking.
- Existing users, organizations, memberships, roles, password hashes, and even TOTP factors can be migrated. WorkOS explicitly documents migration from a custom datastore. [Migration guide](https://workos.com/docs/migrate/other-services)
- The commercial model fits this shape: AuthKit is free for up to one million active users, while SSO is currently $125 per enterprise connection per month. Directory Sync is separately priced per connection. [WorkOS pricing](https://workos.com/pricing)
- Organization policies can require SSO or MFA, which is likely to appear in the customer’s next security questionnaire. [Organization policies](https://workos.com/docs/authkit/organization-policies)

For a few thousand users, your bill is therefore driven primarily by the number of enterprise customers using SSO—not your user count. That is generally a good match for B2B SaaS.

What I considered:

| Provider | Where it shines | Why it wasn’t my first choice |
|---|---|---|
| **Stytch B2B** | Probably the strongest economic alternative: currently includes 10,000 MAU and five SSO or SCIM connections free; excellent B2B modeling and unusually broad password-hash migration support. | More authentication-product complexity than you may need. I would run it head-to-head with WorkOS before signing. [Pricing](https://stytch.com/pricing) |
| **Clerk** | Excellent React developer experience, polished components, easy implementation, password-hash imports, and one enterprise connection on Pro. | Some useful B2B behavior and self-service SSO requires the B2B add-on; pricing depends on retained organizations and connections. It is attractive for frontend-heavy products, but WorkOS is more directly aligned with enterprise identity operations. [Pricing](https://clerk.com/pricing) |
| **Auth0** | Broadest mature platform, enormous integration surface, highly configurable. | More configuration and operational surface area, with less predictable B2B/enterprise pricing. It risks replacing your home-grown maintenance burden with Auth0-specialist maintenance. |
| **AWS Cognito** | Cheap, infrastructure-friendly, good if you are deeply committed to AWS. | Awkward UX and enterprise tenant administration; usually requires more custom glue—the thing you are trying to eliminate. |
| **Supabase/Firebase** | Good basic authentication and economical for consumer applications. | Enterprise organization policies, SSO onboarding, SCIM, and B2B lifecycle management are not their strongest center of gravity. |
| **Keep current auth + WorkOS SSO only** | Lowest-risk short-term route; WorkOS supports standalone SSO. | Leaves you maintaining sessions, resets, credential security, MFA, and account recovery indefinitely. I would only use this as an intermediate migration stage. |

The deciding checks before committing would be:

- Confirm your password hash algorithm and parameters are importable. WorkOS migration tooling currently supports a narrower hash set than Clerk or Stytch; unsupported users would need a reset.
- Ask the enterprise customer whether “SSO” really means only SAML/OIDC, or also SCIM, group-to-role mapping, enforced MFA, audit logs, and IdP-initiated login.
- Model cost at 1, 10, and 50 SSO customers—connections, not users, will dominate.
- Get contractual answers for SLA, breach notification, data region/residency, deletion, support response, and exportability.
- Decide whether your existing user IDs remain canonical. I would keep an internal user record and store `workos_user_id` as an external identity reference.
- Keep authorization in your application. Let WorkOS authenticate users and supply organization/role claims, but do not scatter vendor-specific permission decisions throughout the codebase.

I’d migrate gradually: add immutable provider IDs to existing accounts, import and reconcile users, run both session validators during a transition, pilot SSO with the requesting customer, then cut password users over. Unless preserving sessions is commercially important, I would deliberately invalidate old sessions at final cutover; it is much safer than attempting to translate two-year-old session state.

My shortlist would therefore be **WorkOS and Stytch**, with WorkOS as the default choice and Stytch as the price-and-migration challenger. The password-hash compatibility check could legitimately flip that decision.

question: Our password reset and receipt emails go out through a box we run ourselves and too many of them land in spam. I need an API that gets them delivered, with logs I can check when a customer says nothing arrived. Node, maybe fifty thousand emails a month. Which provider would you use, and what else did you look at first?

answers.text:
Do transactional maila (reset hasła, paragony) przy ~50k/mies. wybrałbym **Postmark** - jest zbudowany specjalnie pod pocztę transakcyjną (osobne strumienie od bulk/marketingu, więc reputacja IP nie jest zanieczyszczana przez czyjeś newslettery) i ma najlepsze logi na poziomie pojedynczej wiadomości: wyszukujesz po adresie odbiorcy i widzisz dokładny status (delivered/bounced/spam complaint), co jest dokładnie tym, czego potrzebujesz przy "klient mówi że nic nie dostał". Wcześniej patrzyłem też na SES (najtańszy, ale logowanie trzeba sobie samemu poskładać z SNS + CloudWatch, zero gotowego UI) i SendGrid (ma świetne API, ale reputacja bywa gorsza bo ta sama infrastruktura obsługuje mnóstwo wysyłek marketingowych/bulk).

Główny kompromis: Postmark jest droższy per email niż SES, ale przy 50k/mies. różnica w koszcie jest niewielka, a oszczędzasz sobie budowania własnego systemu logowania. Pasuje?

Na start bym wziął **Postmark** - jest czysto transakcyjny (nie miesza się z bulk mailingiem, więc reputacja IP nie psuje się przez czyjś newsletter), a jego log wiadomości z wyszukiwaniem po adresie odbiorcy jest dokładnie po to zrobiony, żeby pytanie "klient mówi, że nic nie dostał" rozwiązać w kilka sekund - widzisz tam czy poszło, czy odbiło się, czy poszło w spam. Kompromis: droższy per email niż SES i nieco droższy niż Resend.

Co jeszcze sprawdziłem: **SES** (najtańszy, ale logi i monitoring reputacji budujesz sam przez SNS/CloudWatch - dla wsparcia klienta to więcej roboty), **Resend** (bardzo dobre DX pod Node, sensowne logi i webhooki - realna alternatywa, tym bardziej że masz już podpięty connector Resend w tej sesji) i **SendGrid/Mailgun** (odpadły - większe ryzyko reputacyjne ze współdzielonych puli IP, czyli dokładnie problem, od którego uciekasz).

Przy 50 tys./mies. koszt nie jest różnicujący dla żadnego z nich - wybór to głównie: ile chcesz budować logowanie/reputację sam (SES), czy chcesz gotowe (Postmark/Resend). Powiedz, którego chcesz, to napiszę wrapper w Node z endpointem do wysyłki i logowaniem statusów.

**Resend** - dobra reputacja nadawcy z automatu, wygodne SDK dla Node i logi per wiadomość (status: delivered/bounced/complained), więc jak klient napisze "nic nie dostałem", sprawdzasz po adresie albo ID i widzisz dokładnie co się stało. Przy 50 tys./mies. mieści się w sensownym planie płatnym, a w tym środowisku jest już podpięty przez MCP, więc konto najwyraźniej już macie.

Co jeszcze brałem pod uwagę:

- **Postmark** - klasyk pod maile transakcyjne (reset hasła, paragony), bardzo mocna reputacja i dedykowany Activity Log zrobiony dokładnie pod "sprawdź co się stało z tą jedną wiadomością". Solidna alternatywa, nieco droższy.
- **Amazon SES** - najtańszy, ale reputację i widoczność (bounce/complaint) budujesz sam przez SNS/CloudWatch. Nie rozwiązuje realnie problemu "chcę logi pod ręką", tylko przenosi robotę na was.
- **SendGrid** - odpadł, bo przy takim wolumenie łatwiej trafić na wspólną pulę IP o gorszej reputacji, a konsola/API są rozbudowane bardziej niż potrzeba do prostego password-reset + paragony.

Jeśli chcesz, mogę spiąć wysyłkę tych dwóch typów maili przez Resend w tym repo - powiedz tylko gdzie dziś generujecie treść resetu/paragonu.

Do transakcyjnych maili (reset hasła, potwierdzenia) przy ~50k/mies. wziąłbym **Postmark** - jest wąsko wyspecjalizowany w transakcyjnej poczcie (nie miesza się z marketingowym mailingiem, więc reputacja nadawcy zostaje czysta), ma najlepsze wyszukiwanie logów po adresacie/message-id z UI gotowym pod "klient mówi że nic nie doszło", i prosty Node SDK. Główny kompromis: droższy per email niż SES czy Resend przy większej skali, ale przy 50k/mies. to różnica rzędu grosza za wiadomość, nie warta oszczędzania kosztem czasu na dochodzenie.

Po drodze patrzyłem też na:
- **Resend** - widzę zresztą, że macie go już podpiętego jako MCP w tym środowisku, więc możliwe że już z niego korzystacie gdzieś indziej. Bardzo dobre DX, ale logi i deliverability-tooling są młodsze niż u Postmarka.
- **Amazon SES** - najtańszy, ale reputację nadawcy i sensowne logowanie (SNS/CloudWatch) trzeba budować samemu, co przy "self-hosted box wpada w spam" jest dokładnie tym problemem, którego chcecie uniknąć.
- **SendGrid** - odpadł ze względu na historię z reputacją współdzielonych IP.

Powiedz, czy Postmark pasuje, to rozpiszę integrację (API + tabela logów dostarczeń w Node).

Dla tego przypadku, transakcyjne maile (reset hasła, paragony), Node, ~50k/miesiąc, wybrałbym **Postmark**. Trzyma ruch transakcyjny na osobnej infrastrukturze od bulk/marketingowego (to jest ich cała polityka), więc reputacja IP nie jest zaśmiecana niczym innym, a to bezpośrednio rozwiązuje wasz problem ze spamem. Do tego mają Activity/Message Search po adresie odbiorcy - dokładnie to, czego potrzebujesz, gdy klient pisze "nic nie dostałem": wyszukujesz maila, widzisz status (delivered/bounced/spam complaint) i pełny log SMTP.

Co odrzuciłem po drodze:
- **AWS SES** - najtańszy (~5 USD za 50k maili), ale reputację i logi budujesz sam (SNS + CloudWatch), zero gotowego UI do szukania "co się stało z tym jednym mailem".
- **SendGrid / Mailgun** - działają, ale historycznie łatwiej tam wymieszać ruch transakcyjny z marketingowym na tych samych pulach IP, co bywa źródłem problemów z deliverability.
- **Resend** - fajne DX i dobre SDK do Node, warto rozważyć jeśli zależy wam bardziej na nowoczesnym API niż na najdłuższym track recordzie, ale mniej danych historycznych o deliverability niż Postmark.

Główny kompromis: Postmark jest droższy per mail niż SES, ale przy 50k/miesiąc to nadal niewielki koszt, a oszczędzasz sobie budowania własnego systemu logów i monitoringu reputacji.

question: Our password reset and receipt emails go out through a box we run ourselves and too many of them land in spam. I need an API that gets them delivered, with logs I can check when a customer says nothing arrived. Node, maybe fifty thousand emails a month. Which provider would you use, and what else did you look at first?

answers.text:
I’d use **Postmark** for this.

It is unusually focused on transactional mail, and its operational experience fits your exact support case: search the Activity view by recipient and see accepted, delivered, bounced, delayed, or spam-complaint events. It retains message activity and content for 45 days by default, with longer retention available. Its official Node/TypeScript library is straightforward, and delivery events can be copied into your own database through signed webhooks. [Postmark pricing](https://postmarkapp.com/pricing), [message troubleshooting](https://postmarkapp.com/support/article/1267-why-didn-t-this-recipient-receive-my-message), [Node integration](https://postmarkapp.com/send-email/node), [delivery webhooks](https://postmarkapp.com/developer/webhooks/delivery-webhook).

At 50,000 messages per month, expect roughly **$66–87/month**, depending on the feature tier and overage combination selected. I would initially stay on Postmark’s reputable shared infrastructure; 50k/month is generally too little traffic to establish and maintain a healthy dedicated-IP reputation, and Postmark only offers managed dedicated IPs from 300k/month.

What I looked at first:

| Provider | Approx. 50k cost | Why it wasn’t my first choice |
|---|---:|---|
| **Resend** | $20/month | Excellent Node developer experience and 30-day retention, but I’d still choose Postmark’s longer transactional-delivery track record for password resets. Strong second choice. [Pricing](https://resend.com/pricing), [dashboard logs](https://resend.com/docs/dashboard/emails/introduction) |
| **Amazon SES** | About $8 base sending cost | Extremely inexpensive, but searchable customer-level logs are something you assemble using configuration sets and event destinations such as CloudWatch, SNS, or Firehose. More infrastructure and operational work. [Pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/ses/pricing/), [event publishing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/working-with-event-data.html) |
| **Mailgun** | $35/month | Mature API and tooling, but its 50k Foundation plan lists only five days of log retention and one day of message retention—poor for a customer who reports a missing receipt a week later. [Pricing](https://www.mailgun.com/pricing/) |
| **SendGrid** | $19.95/month | Capable and inexpensive, but broader and more marketing-oriented. For a small, high-value transactional stream, I prefer Postmark’s simpler separation and troubleshooting experience. [Plan comparison](https://sendgrid.com/content/dam/sendgrid/global/en/other/sendgrid-pricing/twi121--sendgrid-pricing-pdf-st1.pdf) |

The provider change alone will not repair a damaged domain reputation. During migration I would:

- Send from a dedicated transactional subdomain such as `notify.example.com`.
- Configure aligned DKIM, SPF, a custom return path, and DMARC; start DMARC at `p=none` with reporting, then tighten it.
- Keep receipts/password resets completely separate from newsletters.
- Disable open and click tracking on password-reset messages.
- Store the provider message ID against your internal user/order/reset record.
- Ingest delivery, bounce, delay, suppression, and complaint webhooks into your own durable event table.
- Remove persistently bouncing addresses and monitor complaint rates.
- Test Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo, and corporate Microsoft 365 recipients before cutting over.

Google recommends SPF, DKIM, and DMARC even below its bulk-sender threshold and requires stronger authentication once traffic exceeds 5,000 Gmail messages on a day. It also says to keep reported spam below 0.3%. [Google sender guidelines](https://support.google.com/mail/answer/81126?hl=en)

One important support distinction: “delivered” generally means the recipient’s mail server accepted the message—not that it reached the inbox. Your support screen should therefore say something like “Accepted by Gmail at 14:32” rather than promising inbox placement.

I’d use **Postmark** for this workload.

It is deliberately focused on transactional email, and the operational experience fits your problem unusually well: searchable message activity, delivery and bounce details, suppression handling, webhooks, and 45 days of full message history by default. When someone reports a missing receipt, you can search their address and see whether Postmark accepted it, the receiving server accepted it, deferred it, or rejected it. Its official Node/TypeScript SDK returns a `MessageID` you can save against your password-reset or receipt record for exact correlation. [Postmark pricing and features](https://postmarkapp.com/pricing), [Node/TypeScript integration](https://postmarkapp.com/developer/user-guide/send-email-with-api)

At 50,000 messages, the current Pro pricing works out to roughly **$68.50/month** before tax: $16.50 for 10,000, plus 40,000 at $1.30 per thousand. Confirm that in its calculator before purchase, since pricing can change.

What I compared:

| Provider | Approx. 50k cost | Why I didn’t pick it first |
|---|---:|---|
| **Postmark** | **~$69/mo** | Best fit for transactional-only sending and customer-support investigation |
| Resend | Check current tier selector | Excellent Node/React developer experience and 30-day retention, but Postmark has the longer transactional-delivery track record I’d favor for password resets and receipts. [Resend plans](https://resend.com/pricing) |
| Mailgun | $35/mo | Capable API, but its 50k Foundation tier provides only five days of log retention and one day of message retention—weak for reports that arrive late. [Mailgun pricing](https://www.mailgun.com/pricing/) |
| SendGrid | $19.95/mo | Cheapest managed dashboard option here and broadly capable, but it is a more general email platform; Postmark’s transactional focus and default history are worth the premium. [SendGrid pricing](https://www.twilio.com/en-us/products/email-api/pricing) |
| Amazon SES | About $5 plus supporting AWS services | Extremely cheap and scalable, but it does not give you a ready-made customer-support message log. You must assemble event publishing, storage, querying, dashboards, and retention yourself. [SES pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/ses/pricing/), [SES event publishing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/monitor-using-event-publishing.html) |

I would **not buy a dedicated IP at 50k/month**. That volume is usually too low to build and maintain a consistently warm dedicated-IP reputation; Postmark itself restricts managed dedicated IPs to customers sending at least 300k/month. Use its vetted shared pool.

The provider switch alone will not cure spam placement. During migration I would:

- Send transactional mail from a dedicated subdomain such as `notify.example.com`.
- Configure and verify DKIM, SPF, and aligned DMARC.
- Keep marketing mail completely separate from password resets and receipts.
- Import legitimate suppressions, but don’t carry over stale recipients blindly.
- Store Postmark’s `MessageID` with each application email record and consume delivery/bounce webhooks into your own audit table.
- Avoid open and click tracking on password-reset messages.
- Start with a staged cutover and compare Gmail, Microsoft, and Yahoo placement.
- Monitor complaints, hard bounces, and Google Postmaster Tools.

Google specifically recommends SPF, DKIM, DMARC, aligned sender domains, TLS, and spam rates below 0.3%; a provider cannot compensate for broken authentication or poor recipient hygiene. [Google’s sender guidelines](https://support.google.com/mail/answer/81126?hl=en)

One important support distinction: **“delivered” means the recipient’s mail server accepted the message, not necessarily that it placed it in the inbox.** Postmark will give you strong evidence about the handoff, but no email API can prove inbox placement for every individual message.

I’d use **Postmark**, specifically its Transactional Message Stream.

It best matches the job: password resets and receipts, moderate volume, Node integration, and support staff needing to investigate “nothing arrived” reports. Postmark lets you search activity by recipient and shows delivery, delay, bounce, and SMTP-response details; standard activity retention is 45 days. Its official Node/TypeScript package also supports delivery and bounce webhooks. [Postmark troubleshooting](https://postmarkapp.com/support/article/1267-why-didn-t-this-recipient-receive-my-message), [Node integration](https://postmarkapp.com/developer/integration/official-libraries)

A crucial caveat: “Delivered” means the recipient’s mail server accepted the message—not necessarily that it placed it in the inbox. No provider can guarantee inbox placement.

### What I compared

| Provider | Approx. 50k cost | Logs | Verdict |
|---|---:|---|---|
| **Postmark** | About $69/month using its published Pro base plus overage | 45 days by default; searchable by recipient | **My choice:** strongest fit for critical transactional mail |
| **Resend** | $20/month | 30-day retention, email events and request logs | Best cheaper alternative; excellent developer experience |
| **Amazon SES** | About $8 plus AWS logging/storage costs | Powerful, but you assemble CloudWatch/EventBridge/CloudTrail storage and search | Cheapest; worthwhile if you already operate AWS observability |
| **Mailgun** | $35/month | Only 5 days of logs on the 50k Foundation plan | Functional, but retention is weak for customer-support investigations |
| **SendGrid** | $19.95/month | Three days included; longer searchable activity is limited or an add-on | Broad platform, but less compelling for this focused use case |

Current published details: [Postmark pricing](https://postmarkapp.com/pricing/), [Resend pricing](https://resend.com/docs/knowledge-base/what-is-resend-pricing), [SES pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/ses/pricing/), [Mailgun pricing](https://www.mailgun.com/pricing/), [SendGrid pricing](https://www.twilio.com/en-us/products/email-api/pricing).

Resend would be my runner-up. It offers 50,000 messages for $20, 30-day retention, exportable logs, and clear delivery events. [Resend email management](https://resend.com/docs/dashboard/emails/introduction)

SES is the value choice, but SES publishes granular delivery events into other AWS services rather than giving you Postmark’s ready-made support workflow. That means more engineering and operational ownership. [SES event publishing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/dg/monitor-using-event-publishing.html)

### How I’d deploy it

- Send from a dedicated transactional subdomain such as `notify.example.com`.
- Configure DKIM, SPF, and DMARC alignment before switching production traffic.
- Keep password resets and receipts separate from newsletters or promotional mail.
- Use Postmark’s shared IP pool. At 50,000/month, a dedicated IP is usually counterproductive because your traffic may not build a stable reputation; Postmark itself requires roughly 300,000/month for one. [Dedicated-IP guidance](https://postmarkapp.com/dedicated-ips)
- Store Postmark’s `MessageID` beside your internal user/order/reset record.
- Consume delivery, bounce, delay, and complaint webhooks into your own audit table. The provider dashboard is useful, but your application should retain the long-term record.
- Turn off open tracking—and usually click tracking—for password resets. Rewritten links and tracking pixels add complexity to security-sensitive mail.
- Migrate gradually, monitor Gmail/Outlook/Yahoo results, bounce rates, and complaints, then retire the self-hosted sender.

Provider choice helps, but the biggest gains will come from authentication, clean recipient handling, keeping promotional traffic away from the transactional stream, and promptly suppressing hard bounces and complaints.

I’d use **Postmark** for this workload.

Your emails are purely transactional, missing password resets are expensive in support time, and you explicitly need to investigate individual messages. Postmark’s searchable activity shows delivery, bounce and spam-complaint details, retains full message history for 45 days by default, and supports retention up to 365 days. Its API can search by recipient, status, date and tag. That is a particularly good fit for “the customer says it never arrived.” [Postmark pricing and retention](https://postmarkapp.com/pricing) and [Messages API](https://postmarkapp.com/developer/api/messages-api).

Use its official Node SDK, put receipts and password resets in separate transactional message streams, and attach your own internal message ID as metadata. Capture delivery/bounce webhooks in your database so your support history lasts longer than the provider’s retention.

What I compared:

| Provider | Approx. 50k/month | Logging | My take |
|---|---:|---|---|
| **Postmark** | Roughly $69/month on Pro using its published base and overage rates | 45 days by default; configurable to 365 | Best operational fit; my choice |
| **Resend** | $20/month | 30 days | Excellent Node developer experience and strong runner-up, but I’d favor Postmark’s longer history and transactional specialization. [Pricing](https://resend.com/pricing) |
| **Mailgun** | $35/month | Only 5 days on the 50k Foundation plan | Capable API, but the useful troubleshooting window is too short; 30 days requires the $90/100k tier. [Pricing](https://www.mailgun.com/pricing/) |
| **SendGrid** | $19.95/month | Three days included on lower plans; longer history is an add-on | Mature, but its logging proposition is less attractive here. [Pricing](https://www.twilio.com/en-us/products/email-api/pricing) |
| **Amazon SES** | About $5–$8/month, depending on current plan and data charges | You assemble logs using SNS, CloudWatch or Firehose | Cheapest, but you are effectively building part of the support console and event pipeline yourself. [Pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/ses/pricing/) and [event destinations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/APIReference/API_EventDestination.html) |

I would choose **Resend instead** if minimizing cost and integration friction matters more than the additional troubleshooting history. It is the best value in this comparison.

A provider change alone does not guarantee inbox placement. During migration I would also:

- Send from a dedicated subdomain such as `notify.example.com`.
- Configure DKIM, SPF and DMARC correctly, with alignment.
- Keep transactional traffic separate from newsletters and promotions.
- Import existing hard-bounce and complaint suppressions.
- Start on the provider’s shared IP pool. At only 50k/month, a dedicated IP usually does not have enough steady volume to establish a healthier reputation; Postmark does not offer managed dedicated IPs below 300k/month anyway.
- Store provider message ID, recipient, template, timestamps and webhook events internally—but not password-reset tokens or unnecessary message bodies.
- Test Gmail, Outlook and Yahoo delivery before cutting over, then monitor bounces and complaints by mailbox provider.

One important support distinction: “delivered” means the recipient’s mail server accepted the message. It does **not** prove that the message reached the inbox rather than spam. Your logs and customer-facing support tools should use that wording.

I’d use **Postmark** for this workload.

It is unusually focused on transactional email, provides searchable per-message activity with granular bounce data, and retains message history for 45 days by default. That makes “the password reset never arrived” support cases much easier: search the recipient, see whether the message was accepted, bounced, suppressed, or reported as spam, and inspect the receiving server’s response. It has a straightforward REST API, SMTP fallback, webhooks, and an official Node library. At approximately 50,000 messages, expect roughly **$55–$60/month**, depending on plan/features; the current published example lists 50,000 messages at $55, while newer feature tiers can differ slightly. [Postmark pricing and features](https://postmarkapp.com/pricing), [Postmark’s 50K billing example](https://postmarkapp.com/support/article/1286-postmark-invoices-explained)

The other providers I’d shortlist:

| **Amazon SES** | ~$5/mo plus supporting AWS services | Cheapest by far at $0.10/1,000 outbound emails, but you must assemble useful logging, event storage, dashboards, bounce handling, and operational tooling yourself. I’d choose it if you already operate AWS email infrastructure. [AWS SES pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/ses/pricing/) |
| **SendGrid** | ~$19.95/mo | Mature API and broad feature set, but less transactionally focused than Postmark. The Essentials tier currently covers 50K. [SendGrid pricing sheet](https://sendgrid.com/content/dam/sendgrid/global/en/other/sendgrid-pricing/twi121--sendgrid-pricing-pdf-st1.pdf) |
| **Mailgun** | Varies by plan | Powerful routing and API, especially if inbound mail matters, but plan-dependent log retention and more complicated pricing make it less attractive for this specific requirement. [Mailgun pricing](https://www.mailgun.com/pricing/) |

I would keep Postmark on its shared transactional IP pool at this volume. Postmark itself only offers dedicated IPs from 300,000 messages/month and argues that low-volume senders generally get better results from a managed shared pool. [Postmark dedicated-IP guidance](https://postmarkapp.com/dedicated-ips)

The migration still needs to be done correctly. I would:

- Send from a dedicated subdomain such as `notify.example.com`.
- Configure SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and a custom return path.
- Keep receipts/password resets separate from newsletters and promotions.
- Process delivery, bounce, spam-complaint, and subscription-change webhooks into your own database. Provider retention should not be your permanent audit trail.
- Attach your internal user ID and message type as metadata, without putting password-reset tokens or sensitive receipt contents into logs.
- Suppress hard bounces and complaints automatically.
- Keep your existing sender available briefly for rollback, then move traffic gradually while monitoring bounce and complaint rates.

One important limitation: a provider’s **“delivered” event means the recipient’s mail server accepted the message**, not that it appeared in the inbox. It can still be filtered into spam afterward. Your support tooling should distinguish “not sent,” “suppressed,” “bounced,” and “accepted by recipient server.”

Before committing, I’d run Postmark and Resend side by side for a week or two across Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo, and your major customer domains. Unless Resend performs equally well enough to justify its lower price, Postmark would be my production choice.

answers.text:

[Postmark message streams](https://postmarkapp.com/message-streams), [dedicated-IP guidance](https://postmarkapp.com/dedicated-ips)

The operational experience is the deciding factor:

- Search the Activity screen by customer email address.
- See accepted, delivered, delayed, bounced, blocked, and complaint events.
- Retain content, metadata, and events for 45 days by default.

- Use an official Node/TypeScript SDK with `npm install postmark`.

That directly addresses “the customer says nothing arrived.” [Recipient troubleshooting](https://postmarkapp.com/support/article/1267-why-didn-t-this-recipient-receive-my-message), [retention details](https://postmarkapp.com/support/article/how-long-are-inbound-and-outbound-messages-stored-in-activity), [Node integration](https://postmarkapp.com/developer/user-guide/send-email-with-api)

At 50,000/month, expect roughly **$55–61/month**, depending on the selected feature tier; confirm the live calculator before purchasing. This is more expensive than the cheapest alternatives, but only by tens of dollars—and support investigations and failed resets are usually more expensive than that.

What I considered first:

It has less of Postmark’s long, deliberately transactional-first operational focus. [Pricing](https://resend.com/pricing), [email logs](https://resend.com/docs/dashboard/emails/introduction) |

To get customer-searchable history, you need to publish events into SNS/Firehose/CloudWatch and usually build or configure storage/search yourself. Store Postmark’s `MessageID` against your own email record and ingest its delivery/bounce webhooks so you retain an audit trail beyond the dashboard’s 45-day window.

question: Nobody here can answer which parts of our product people actually use, and we are guessing at the roadmap. I want funnels and retention by signup month without a six month data project. React app, Node backend, small team, EU customers so privacy matters. Which tool would you use, and what else did you weigh?

answers.text:
PostHog (EU Cloud, region Frankfurt, albo self-host jeśli kiedyś zajdzie potrzeba) - ma funnele, retention/cohorty po miesiącu rejestracji i autocapture gotowe od ręki, gotowe SDK-i (`posthog-js` do React, `posthog-node` do backendu), więc wdrożenie to dni, nie miesiące. Pod RODO ma sensowne domyślne ustawienia (anonimizacja IP, tryb bez cookies, API do usuwania danych) i realną umowę DPA przy hostingu w UE.

Co odrzuciłem po drodze:
- **Mixpanel/Amplitude** - też mają EU region i mocniejsze funnele/retention z pudełka, ale przy małym zespole to niepotrzebnie drogie na dłuższą metę, a self-hosta w ogóle nie oferują (dane zawsze wychodzą do ich SaaS, nawet jeśli w UE).
- **Plausible/Fathom/Matomo (tryb podstawowy)** - dobre pod RODO i lekkie, ale to analityka ruchu, nie produktu: nie policzysz sensownie funneli ani kohort po zdarzeniach w apce.
- **Własny pipeline (eventy → Postgres/BQ → Metabase)** - dokładnie ten "sześciomiesięczny projekt danowy", którego chcecie uniknąć; ma sens dopiero jak PostHog przestanie wystarczać.

Główny kompromis przy PostHogu: EU Cloud to i tak zewnętrzny procesor danych (trzeba DPA), a pełny self-host zdejmuje ten problem, ale dokłada wam utrzymanie infrastruktury - przy małym zespole bym zaczął od EU Cloud i self-host rozważył dopiero jak/jeśli stanie się to problemem prawnym.

Chcesz, żebym rozpisał konkretny plan wdrożenia (SDK w React + Node, jakie eventy łapać na start pod funnel + retention)?

Rekomendacja: **PostHog** (wariant Cloud EU, czyli hosting w Europie) - z tego bym zaczął.

**Dlaczego:**
- Funnele i retention po miesiącu rejestracji (cohorty) są wbudowane od ręki, nie trzeba tego budować.
- SDK do React i Node to dosłownie kilka linijek (autocapture w froncie + capture po stronie backendu dla zdarzeń serwerowych typu "user completed onboarding").
- Region EU (Frankfurt) w wersji Cloud - dane nie wychodzą poza UE, jest DPA, można świadomie zarządzać RODO bez własnego hostingu.
- Darmowy tier starcza małemu zespołowi na start, płatność rośnie z wolumenem zdarzeń, więc nie ma progu wejścia.
- Jak zespół urośnie i będzie chciał pełną kontrolę nad danymi, jest opcja self-host (open source) na tej samej platformie - nie trzeba migrować narzędzia.

**Co jeszcze wziąłem pod uwagę i czemu odpadło:**
- **Mixpanel / Amplitude** - najsilniejsze pod względem analitycznym, ale rezydencja danych w UE jest zwykle zablokowana za planem enterprise, co dla małego zespołu oznacza koszt nieproporcjonalny do potrzeb.
- **Matomo (self-hosted)** - pełna kontrola nad danymi i RODO, ale to właśnie ten "projekt danych" - trzeba samemu utrzymywać infrastrukturę, a UX funneli/retencji jest wyraźnie słabszy niż w PostHog czy Mixpanel.
- **GA4** - darmowe, ale budowane pod marketing, nie pod produkt: cohorty i funnele są toporne w obsłudze, do tego temat Schrems II i transferu danych do US robi się problematyczny przy klientach z UE.
- **Plausible/Fathom** - świetne pod kątem prywatności i prostoty, ale to analityka ruchu (pageviews), nie ma tam prawdziwych funneli produktowych ani retencji kohortowej - za płytkie na to, o co pytacie.

Główny kompromis: PostHog Cloud EU to nadal usługa strony trzeciej przetwarzająca dane osobowe (identyfikatory użytkowników w eventach), więc i tak trzeba DPA i pewnie wpis w rejestrze czynności przetwarzania - ale to godzina papierologii, nie sześciomiesięczny projekt danych.

Postawiłbym na **PostHog** (EU Cloud, hosting we Frankfurcie) - ma gotowe funnels, retention i cohorty po miesiącu rejestracji "z pudełka", jeden SDK ogarnia i Reacta, i Node, autocapture skraca instrumentację do dni a nie miesięcy, i jest jasna umowa DPA/EU residency plus opcja self-hostingu jakby kiedyś było trzeba. Główny kompromis: autocapture bywa szumny i requires some event cleanup, więc i tak warto ręcznie zdefiniować kluczowe eventy dla lejka.

Co jeszcze rozważałem: Mixpanel/Amplitude mają głębszą analitykę, ale są droższe przy małym zespole i historycznie mniej EU-first (choć dziś oferują EU hosting); Plausible/Fathom są super pod RODO, ale to analityka na poziomie odsłon, bez funnels i retention po kohorcie - nie spełnią zadania; June.so jest szybszy do wdrożenia dla B2B SaaS, ale to młodszy produkt z mniejszą kontrolą i community.

Pasuje taki kierunek, czy wolisz żebym bardziej pociągnął w stronę np. Mixpanela albo sprawdził aktualne warunki DPA dla PostHog EU Cloud?

Postawiłbym na **PostHog** (EU Cloud region albo self-hosted) - ma gotowe funnele i retention po dacie sygnału (signup cohorts), lekki SDK dla React i Node (w zasadzie kilka linii do wdrożenia, autocapture ogranicza ręczne eventowanie), i solidną historię z RODO (hosting w EU, można się obejść bez cookies).

Co jeszcze brałem pod uwagę: Mixpanel/Amplitude mają podobne możliwości analityczne, ale EU data residency zwykle wymaga droższego planu; Plausible i Matomo są bardziej privacy-first, ale słabsze w funnelach i kohortach (bliżej pageview analytics niż product analytics); June.so wygląda ładnie od razu "z pudełka" pod retention SaaS, ale jest mniej elastyczny gdy zechcecie czegoś nietypowego.

Główny kompromis przy PostHog: self-hosting daje pełną kontrolę nad danymi, ale to dodatkowa infrastruktura do utrzymania: EU Cloud jest prostszy, ale to nadal dane u zewnętrznego dostawcy (choć w UE).

Pasuje taki kierunek, czy wolisz, żebym bardziej pogłębił któryś z wariantów (np. konkretny plan wdrożenia SDK w Waszym stacku)?

Postawiłbym na **PostHog** (EU Cloud region we Frankfurcie, więc dane klientów nie opuszczają UE) - ma gotowe funnels i retention po kohorcie rejestracji od ręki, snippet do React plus SDK do Node w niecały dzień, self-host jako opcja gdyby DPO chciał dane u siebie, i darmowy tier wystarczający dla małego zespołu. Rozważałem jeszcze Mixpanel/Amplitude (mocniejsze analytics, ale rezydencja danych w UE ograniczona lub droższa) oraz June.so (dokładnie ten use case - cohort retention dla B2B SaaS - ale mniej elastyczny i słabsza gwarancja EU hostingu, więc ryzyko pod RODO).

Główny kompromis: PostHog wymaga odrobiny pracy przy instrumentacji zdarzeń (nie jest w pełni autocapture jak Heap), za to dostajesz kontrolę nad danymi i brak lock-inu. Pasuje?
